title: CVE-2026-39816 Allows Privesc And Code Execution In Apache NiFi
summary: ZeroPath Research discovered CVE-2026-39816 in Apache NiFi: when the optional nifi-other-graph-services-nar bundle is installed, authenticated users without the EXECUTE_CODE privilege can run arbitrary code on the NiFi server via ExecuteGraphQuery against a TinkerPop target. Affects NiFi >= 2.0.0-M1 and < 2.9.0; patched in 2.9.0.
body_text:
Summary ZeroPath Research discovered a vulnerability in Apache NiFi that allows authenticated users without the EXECUTE_CODE privilege to execute arbitrary code on the NiFi server if administrators have installed the optional nifi-other-graph-services-nar NAR. The issue was tracked in NIFI-15800 and patched in version 2.9.0. MITRE has assigned it CVE-2026-39816 , and scored the severity as "high." Using our POC to get a shell on a NiFi server. Impacted Software Vulnerable Versions Patched Versions >= 2.0.0-M1, < 2.9.0 >= 2.9.0 Timeline 2026-04-03 — Issue reported to Apache NiFi maintainers 2026-04-07 — NIFI-15800 created to track the issue 2026-04-10 — NiFi 2.9.0 ships with a patch POC Full working POC with Docker setup to produce a vulnerable environment to test against. Apache NiFi Background Apache NiFi is an open source dataflow management system that allows users to create, execute and manage data pipelines. It's similar to Airflow or Dagster, but instead of orchestrating batch jobs that other systems execute, NiFi sits in the data path itself, transforming and routing data as it passes from one place to another, typically in real-time continuous flows. The project has 6.1k stars on Github, and is widely-used across the industry. 6.1k stars as of April 28th, 2026. Typically, NiFi is not exposed to the public internet, but 302 publicly-accessible instances do show up in Shodan. 302 publicly-accessible NiFi instances as of April 28th, 2026. Users primarily interact with NiFi via a web UI, where they can create and edit dataflows by drag and dropping components on a canvas. Screenshot of NiFi canvas from its user guide . Privilege Model Given that NiFi exists to author and manage data flows, its users have a fair amount of privilege by default compared to something like a word processor. However, executing arbitrary code is gated behind a specific permission. By design, there are intended to be flow designers who can't run whatever they want on the server. NiFi does not have pre-defined roles. Instead, user privilege is constructed by assigning one or more granular permissions. The full list (especially the EXECUTE_CODE permission) will become relevant later: Permission Effect EXECUTE_CODE Processors that compile/run user-supplied code (ExecuteScript, ExecuteGroovyScript, ...) READ_FILESYSTEM Reading from the local filesystem (GetFile, FetchFile) WRITE_FILESYSTEM Writing to the local filesystem (PutFile) READ_DISTRIBUTED_FILESYSTEM Reading HDFS-style remote stores WRITE_DISTRIBUTED_FILESYSTEM Writing HDFS-style remote stores ACCESS_KEYTAB Kerberos keytab access ACCESS_TICKET_CACHE Kerberos ticket cache access ACCESS_ENVIRONMENT_CREDENTIALS Reading credentials from env vars / credential providers EXPORT_NIFI_DETAILS Exporting NiFi internals (e.g. flow definition with secrets) REFERENCE_REMOTE_RESOURCES Fetching arbitrary URLs (InvokeHTTP, etc.) CVE-2026-39816: Running code without EXECUTE_CODE Overview NiFi contains two processors for executing traversals against graph databases: ExecuteGraphQuery and ExecuteGraphQueryRecord. Neither require EXECUTE_CODE to instantiate or run... and for good reason at first glance. Executing a traversal, like executing a SQL query, intuitively feels like an operation that shouldn't involve arbitrary code execution. However, if the traversal target is a Tinkerpop-compatible service, this common sense assumption fails: under some circumstances the user can specify a query using arbitrary Groovy code, which is then run on the NiFi server. NiFi Graph Extensions NiFi has a large ecosystem of first and third party extensions that add functionality. The core functionality is kept fairly lean by design. Most of these extensions are actually part of the NiFi project, and live in the main NiFi repo . It's normal to add extensions to support access to particular data sources for example (e.g. Airtable or Dropbox). If users want to run graph traversals against TinkerPop-compatible graph databases, they must enable a number of first party extensions from the NiFi project. To be vulnerable to CVE-2026-39816, those must include: nifi-graph-nar adds the ExecuteGraphQuery and ExecuteGraphQueryRecord processors for making graph queries nifi-graph-client-service-api-nar adds GraphClientService, the abstraction that different graph db clients implement nifi-other-graph-services Adds TinkerpopClientService, the specific implementation of GraphClientService for TinkerPop-compatible graph dbs TinkerPop Query Conventions ExecuteGraphQuery and ExecuteGraphQueryRecord both allow the user to specify a graph client, and a query to run. TinkerpopClientService is one possible graph client. TinkerpopClientService is interesting though, because TinkerPop has an unusual approach to traversals: while users can specify them as strings, the preferred technique is to implement the query directly in the language you're using with Gremlin Language Variants like this: Cluster cluster = Cluster . open ( "conf/remote.yaml" ) ; GraphTraversalSource g = AnonymousTraversalSource . traversal ( ) . with ( DriverRemoteConnection . using ( cluster ) ) ; g // GraphTraversalSource - the entry point . V ( ) // GraphTraversal<Vertex,Vertex> (start step) . has ( 'name' , 'alice' ) // GraphTraversal<Vertex,Vertex> (filter step) . out ( 'knows' ) // GraphTraversal<Vertex,Vertex> (nav step) . toList ( ) // terminal: triggers execution, returns List Here the traversal is the bit after "g," but each step of the path is expressed using a native Groovy method. Per the TinkerPop documentation , this approach is preferred for a number of reasons, including: Queries are compile-time verified Queries can be composed just like any other functions Development-time linting can flag errors and so on The Flaw: TinkerPop's Unorthodox Query Approach Breaks Assumptions TinkerpopClientService, NiFi's abstraction for executing TinkerPop traversals against a target, supports both the string-based expression of traversals AND the preferred native language approach. String-based submission is the default, but the service can be instantiated with native language submission like this: "properties" : { "Script Submission Type" : "bytecode-submission" , "Settings Specification" : "service-settings" , "Contact Points" : args.gremlin_host , "Port" : args.gremlin_port , "Path" : "/gremlin" } It's important to note here, that "bytecode" does not refer to JVM-bytecode... TinkerPop has its own bytecode that traversals in supported languages get compiled down to. It is much less full featured than something like JVM bytecode... potentially abusable because it supports arbitrary lambdas, but getting a shell is a little bit harder than instantiating ProcessBuilder. However, if we look at how TinkerPopClient actually handles these bytecode submissions, something interesting jumps out: protected Map < String , String > bytecodeSubmission ( String s , Map < String , Object > map , GraphQueryResultCallback graphQueryResultCallback ) { // ... Script compiled ; // ... // ZP !!! compile groovy code that will ultimately become TinkerPop bytecode compiled = groovyShell . parse ( s ) ; groovyShell here has the type groovy.lang.GroovyShell . The real input to the bytecode submission vector is Groovy code, which is compiled and run on the NiFi server to produce the bytecode to send to TinkerPop. This makes executing arbitrary code easy. We just need to create an ExecuteGraphQuery processor and set the query to valid Groovy code that returns a HashMap, e.g.: GROOVY_PAYLOAD = ( 'def idOut = "id".execute().text.trim()
' 'def hostnameOut = "hostname".execute().text.trim()
' 'def proof = "RCE_PROOF\nid: " + idOut + "\nhostname: " + hostnameOut
' f'new File(" { MARKER_FILE } ").text = proof
' 'def result = new HashMap()
' 'result.put("rce_proof", "CONFIRMED")
' 'result' ) This is only a security issue ultimately because ExecuteGraphQuery and related components can be instantiated by a user without EXECUTE_CODE permissions, potentially because executing graph queries under most circumstances doesn't involve arbitrary code execution. This TinkerPop edge case invalidates some core intuitive security assumptions likely made by the NiFi developers. Mitigation Upgrade Apache NiFi to 2.9.0 or later If upgrade is not possible, ensure the following optional extensions are not installed: nifi-graph-nar nifi-graph-client-service-api-nar nifi-other-graph-services Takeaways There's no buffer overflow here... no SQL query that interpolates unsanitized input, no insecure deserialization. The issue exists purely at the semantic level: the ExecuteGraphQuery and related components were gated by one set of required privileges, but in actual practice supported behavior typically only available under another. As a result, this is a hard vulnerability to find with a traditional SAST tool in an application that is filled with by-design code execution vectors. LLMs working within a structured scaffold made it much easier to pick out the one code execution path that was surprising given the meaning of the permissions required to access it.

title: Top 10 Bizzabo Competitors & Alternatives for Enterprise Events in 2026
summary: Compare the best Bizzabo competitors for enterprise events in 2026. Honest reviews, pricing, offline check-in capabilities, and migration tips included.
body_text: Events Posted on May 27, 2026 Bizzabo is a good platform. Gartner named it a Magic Quadrant Leader two years running. Forrester put it in their Wave as a Leader. The Klik SmartBadge technology is clever — it tracks networking interactions, delivers sponsor ROI data, and gives your check-in process a premium feel. If you already use Bizzabo, you probably know all of that. You’re here because something isn’t working. Maybe it’s the pricing that keeps climbing every time you add another event to your contract. Maybe it’s the moment your registration team realized Klik SmartBadges need a constant internet connection — and your venue’s WiFi just went down in front of 3,000 people waiting to check in. Or maybe you’re in a regulated industry where hosting attendee data on shared cloud infrastructure isn’t going to fly with your compliance team. Whatever brought you here, you’re not alone. More enterprise event teams are evaluating Bizzabo competitors in 2026 than at any point in the platform’s history. And when you look at why, a pattern shows up: pricing that gets complicated at scale, onsite gaps for teams running large in-person events, and slower AI innovation compared to newer platforms. We built this guide for enterprise event managers, conference directors, VPs of marketing ops, and event operations leads at Fortune 500 and mid-market companies. It’s not a generic listicle where every platform sounds the same. We actually dug into what each Bizzabo alternative does well, where it falls short, and — this is the part no other comparison covers — which platforms keep working when your venue’s WiFi doesn’t. For a direct head-to-head, you can also check out our full InEvent vs Bizzabo comparison . This guide compares the top 10 Bizzabo competitors for enterprise events in 2026, with special focus on offline check-in capabilities, data security, CRM integrations, and migration guidance. Table of Contents Toggle Why Enterprise Event Teams Are Exploring Bizzabo Alternatives in 2026 The intro covered the “what.” Now let’s talk about the “why.” When you dig into the reasons enterprise teams start shopping for Bizzabo alternatives, three things come up over and over again. Pricing That Gets Complicated Fast Bizzabo doesn’t publish its pricing. You have to talk to sales to get a number ( Bizzabo pricing page ). That alone is a friction point for procurement teams who want to compare options before getting on a call. From what’s publicly available, Bizzabo uses a seat-based pricing model starting around $499 per user per month, billed annually ( Vendr ). That’s roughly $6,000 per user per year. For a team of three, you’re already looking at $18,000 before you’ve added a single feature. And that’s where it gets tricky. Customized branding, API access, advanced virtual capabilities, CRM integrations, the Onsite Command App, and video on demand are all listed as add-ons ( Vendr ). One Vendr user reported that Bizzabo increased their Premium Package price by 20% at renewal ( Vendr ). G2 reviewers note that while the platform offers strong value, additional features can increase costs in ways that are hard to predict when you’re budgeting for a full calendar of events ( G2 — Bizzabo Pricing ). For enterprise teams running 10 or more events a year, those add-ons stack up. And when you can’t see the final number until you’re deep in a sales conversation, it makes it hard to do a clean side-by-side comparison with competitors who price more transparently. In-Person Event Gaps That Show Up Onsite Bizzabo was built for B2B marketing conferences. That’s its DNA. And for that use case — tracking marketing attribution, syncing with your CRM, proving event ROI to leadership — it’s strong. But enterprise events aren’t always tidy marketing conferences in well-connected hotels. They happen in convention centers where shared WiFi buckles under load. Government facilities with restricted networks. Pharmaceutical campuses where guest internet is locked down. Military installations where you’re lucky to get cellular signal. This is where Bizzabo’s architecture hits a wall. Klik SmartBadges — their signature onsite product — need a persistent internet connection to transmit the networking and engagement data they collect ( Bizzabo pricing page — Onsite features ). If your venue WiFi goes down during the 8 AM check-in rush, those badges can’t sync. And Bizzabo doesn’t offer a native offline check-in system that caches data locally and syncs when connectivity returns. Capterra reviewers also flag that setting up events can be “very lengthy” and that connecting to badge printers “gets a lot more complicated” ( Capterra — Bizzabo Reviews ). Multiple G2 reviews describe the platform as occasionally feeling “rigid” when you try to customize beyond its default setup ( G2 — Bizzabo Pricing ). For enterprise ops teams who need to move fast onsite, that rigidity costs time. AI Features That Haven’t Kept Pace Bizzabo launched its Event OS Copilot in late 2024 — a generative AI tool that helps with event content creation and planning ( Event Industry News, November 2024 ). It’s a solid start. But newer platforms have moved faster. Some now offer AI-powered registration builders where you type a command and the form builds itself. Others have shipped facial recognition check-in, AI-driven attendee matchmaking, automated agenda generation, AI email verification, and platform-wide ChatGPT integrations that work across emails, websites, speaker bios, and event apps. Bizzabo’s CRM integrations remain a strength — Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, and Eloqua all connect natively ( Bizzabo pricing page ). But when it comes to the AI tools that enterprise event teams are starting to expect in 2026, Bizzabo is playing catch-up while newer competitors are shipping features monthly. Enterprise event teams are exploring Bizzabo alternatives primarily because of pricing complexity at scale, limited offline onsite capabilities, and slower AI feature adoption compared to newer platforms. What Enterprise Teams Should Look for in a Bizzabo Competitor Before we get into the platforms, let’s set the criteria. Not every event management platform is built for enterprise. And the features that matter when you’re running a 200-person workshop are very different from the ones that matter when you’re managing a 3,000-person multi-track summit across three days. Here are the nine things worth evaluating before you sign anything. Offline check-in with local server sync. This is the one most people don’t think about until it’s too late. Can the platform check in attendees, print badges, and track session attendance when venue WiFi drops? Does it cache data locally on the device and auto-sync everything once connectivity comes back? If your events happen in convention centers, government buildings, or international venues with unreliable internet — this isn’t optional. It’s the difference between a smooth registration and a line out the door. Enterprise-grade security. Your compliance team will ask about this. Look for SOC 2 Type II certification, GDPR compliance, ISO 27001, encrypted data storage , and single sign-on via Azure AD or Okta. If the platform can’t show you these certifications upfront, that’s a red flag for any organization handling sensitive attendee data. Private cloud or dedicated hosting. Some organizations — especially in government, defense, and healthcare — can’t put attendee data on shared cloud infrastructure. Can the platform run on a dedicated Azure or AWS instance? Can it sit inside your organization’s own governance structure? For more on why this matters, check out our guide to private cloud hosting for events . Multi-track agenda management. Enterprise summits don’t run one session at a time. They run 5 to 15 parallel tracks with overlapping schedules, room changes, and last-minute swaps. The platform needs a drag-and-drop agenda builder that syncs in real time across the event app, the website, and any digital signage in the venue. If your team has to manually update three places every time a speaker changes rooms, that’s a problem. Native CRM integrations. Not Zapier workarounds. Not middleware that breaks when someone updates a field. Direct, native connectors for Salesforce, HubSpot, Dynamics 365, Marketo, and Veeva. Your marketing ops team needs event data flowing into the CRM without manual exports and CSV uploads. Hybrid and virtual delivery built in. If the platform’s virtual event capability is a third-party tool bolted on through an integration, you’ll feel it. Look for native streaming, recording, breakout rooms, and a virtual lobby that lives inside the same system as your registration and analytics. Bolted-on virtual always means disconnected data. White-label branding. Your attendees should see your brand, not the platform’s. Full customization of registration pages, the event app, email communications, onsite kiosks, and printed badges. If the platform’s logo shows up anywhere in the attendee experience, that’s a dealbreaker for enterprise conferences where brand consistency matters. Transparent pricing. Can you get a ballpark number without a three-week sales cycle? Do you know what you’ll actually pay before you sign the contract — including add-ons, overages, and hardware costs? After what we covered in the pricing section above, you already know why this matters. Dedicated human support. Not a chatbot. Not a help center link. A named project manager who knows your event, your team, and your timeline. For large-scale international summits and multi-day conferences, having a dedicated PM who picks up the phone when something goes wrong onsite is the difference between a minor hiccup and a full operational meltdown. Look for platforms that also offer onsite support crews — not just remote troubleshooting. Keep this checklist open. And while the onsite tools are mature, they lack some of the innovations (AI check-in, facial recognition, NFC/RFID gamification) that newer platforms like InEvent have shipped. The table above compares the top 10 Bizzabo competitors across offline check-in capability, CRM integrations, AI features, security compliance, pricing, and G2 ratings for enterprise event teams evaluating alternatives in 2026. Why Offline Check-In with Local Server Sync Is the Enterprise Feature Most Platforms Miss If you’ve read through the comparison table above, one column probably stood out. Under Offline Check-In, InEvent is the only platform with a full green checkmark. Everyone else is either limited, partial, or a flat no. This section explains why that matters more than most buyers realize until it’s too late. The Problem Nobody Talks About Convention centers, hotel ballrooms, government facilities, pharmaceutical campuses, military bases, and international venues in developing markets all share one thing: WiFi that works fine during the site visit and fails under actual event load. Here’s the scenario. It’s 8:00 AM. Your opening keynote starts at 9:00. You have 2,000 attendees arriving in a 45-minute window. They’re scanning QR codes, printing badges, confirming session assignments. Every check-in transaction hits your cloud-based event platform. And then the WiFi drops. Maybe it’s the venue’s shared network buckling under load from three simultaneous events. Maybe it’s a government facility where guest internet access is restricted by design. Maybe it’s a resort in Southeast Asia or Latin America where the infrastructure just isn’t built for that kind of bandwidth. When your check-in system depends entirely on cloud connectivity, one router failure turns your 10-second-per-person badge process into a manual paper-list scramble. The line backs up. Attendees get frustrated. Your registration team starts writing names on blank badges by hand. Your client’s executive team walks in to a lobby that looks like a disorganized mess. For enterprise events, this isn’t a minor inconvenience. It’s a brand-damaging operational failure that gets remembered long after the keynote ends. How InEvent’s Local Server Sync Works InEvent built its onsite check-in system to work without the internet. That’s not a workaround or a backup mode — it’s a core architecture decision. When your team sets up InEvent’s check-in stations with Zebra printers for badge printing , the system caches attendee data locally on each device. If venue WiFi drops during peak arrival, staff continue scanning attendees, verifying registrations, and printing badges from the local cache exactly as if the connection were still live. No pause. No paper lists. No manual workarounds. Once connectivity is restored, all check-in records — every scan, every badge print, every session assignment — sync back automatically to the cloud platform. Nothing gets lost. Your analytics are complete. Your post-event reports are accurate. The attendee experience during that WiFi outage? Indistinguishable from a normal check-in. This matters beyond just speed. For organizations that need to maintain tight data security and encrypted data storage standards, knowing that attendee records are cached locally — not lost in a failed network transmission — protects data integrity in exactly the scenarios where other platforms create gaps. Teams running events that require private cloud hosting or dedicated infrastructure will recognize why this architecture matters: the system doesn’t depend on a single point of failure. The hardware side is fully integrated, too. InEvent’s onsite check-in works with Zebra ZD200, ZD400, and ZD600 series printers, Brother printers, self-service iPad kiosks, and NFC/RFID wearable badges. The badge printing system supports on-demand printing in multiple badge formats — plastic, paper, PVC — with drag-and-drop design tools and direct printer integration. And if you need human backup, InEvent deploys onsite mobile printing crews for high-volume events. Why Bizzabo Can’t Do This This isn’t a criticism of Bizzabo’s product quality. It’s a recognition of architectural design choices. Bizzabo’s Klik SmartBadges are genuinely innovative. Attendees tap badges to exchange contact information, visit sponsor booths, and generate networking data that feeds back into Bizzabo’s analytics. It’s a clever product that delivers sponsor ROI data that most traditional badges can’t. But Klik badges need a persistent internet connection to transmit that interaction data. If your venue WiFi drops, the badges can’t sync. The networking features they’re designed for stop working. And Bizzabo’s broader onsite check-in and badge printing workflow also relies on cloud connectivity — there’s no native local cache that continues operating independently during an outage. For events in well-connected urban hotels with dedicated WiFi, this is rarely a problem. But for enterprise teams running events in the kinds of venues we listed above — government buildings, pharma campuses, military installations, convention centers at peak load, international venues with unreliable infrastructure — this architectural gap becomes a real operational risk. Who Needs Offline Check-In Most Not every event needs this. If you’re running a 200-person dinner in a hotel ballroom with strong WiFi, cloud-dependent check-in is fine. But for these teams, offline capability isn’t optional: Government and military event planners who run events in secure facilities with restricted or nonexistent guest WiFi. If your events touch public procurement requirements , you already know that network access can’t be assumed. Pharmaceutical companies hosting events on research campuses where guest internet is locked down by IT security policy — and the event team has no authority to change that. International event teams managing conferences in Latin America, Southeast Asia, Africa, and other markets where venue internet infrastructure varies wildly between cities and sometimes between floors of the same building. Convention centers during peak load periods, when three or four events are sharing the same network and the WiFi vendor promised bandwidth they can’t actually deliver. And any organization where a check-in failure at scale — a visible, public, brand-damaging line out the door — is simply not an acceptable outcome. If that describes your events, the Offline Check-In column in the table above just became the most important column in your evaluation. How to Migrate from Bizzabo to a New Platform Without Losing Data Switching event platforms is one of those projects that sounds simple until you’re halfway through it. Registration data, CRM integrations, email automation rules, historical reporting — it all needs to move without breaking. And if you’re mid-contract with Bizzabo or have a flagship event coming up in the next quarter, the timing adds pressure. The good news: Bizzabo migrations don’t have to be painful. Here’s a five-step process that enterprise teams use to switch platforms without losing data or disrupting their event calendar. Step 1 — Audit Your Current Bizzabo Setup Start by exporting everything you’ll need from Bizzabo before you cancel anything. Pull your attendee databases, email templates, registration form configurations, and historical event data. Document which integrations you’re actively using — Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Eloqua, any Zapier workflows you’ve built. If you’ve been using Klik SmartBadges, identify which data you need to preserve. Networking interaction logs, session attendance records, and sponsor engagement metrics are all valuable for year-over-year benchmarking. Export these before your contract ends, because access goes away when the subscription does. Step 2 — Map Your Must-Have Features Against the Checklist Go back to the enterprise checklist from Section 3 and use it as your evaluation framework. But don’t just look for features your new platform adds — make sure it also covers what Bizzabo already handled well for you. If Bizzabo’s marketing attribution, CRM sync, or branded event page builder were core to your workflow, confirm your shortlisted replacement covers those at the same level. This is the step where most teams catch gaps early. Better to discover that a platform lacks a feature during evaluation than two weeks before your annual conference. Step 3 — Run a Parallel Pilot Event Don’t switch cold. This is the single most important piece of migration advice. Run one smaller event — an internal meeting, a regional roadshow, a client dinner — on the new platform while keeping Bizzabo active for your flagship conference. This lets your team learn the new system’s registration builder, email workflows, and check-in process without putting your highest-stakes event at risk. It also gives your IT team time to test CRM integrations and data flows in a lower-pressure environment. Most enterprise teams run parallel for one to two event cycles before fully migrating. Step 4 — Migrate Registration Data and Integrations The data migration itself is usually more straightforward than people expect. Most modern platforms accept CSV imports for attendee databases, and many can map custom fields during import. Where it gets more interesting is the integration layer. If you’ve been running CRM sync through Zapier or middleware with Bizzabo, migration is an opportunity to simplify. InEvent, for example, has native connectors for Salesforce, HubSpot, Dynamics 365, and Marketo — which means the Zapier workarounds you built to bridge gaps in Bizzabo can be replaced with direct integrations. That’s fewer failure points and cleaner data. Test your email automation rules, registration confirmation workflows, and CRM field mappings thoroughly before going live. Run test registrations through the full flow. Check that data appears correctly in your CRM. Send test emails. The 30 minutes you spend testing saves hours of troubleshooting during a live event. Step 5 — Train Your Team and Go Live The onboarding experience varies dramatically across platforms. Some hand you a knowledge base link and wish you luck. Others assign a named project manager who walks your team through every workflow. InEvent assigns a dedicated project manager and account manager for every enterprise onboarding. Their team has supported migrations from Bizzabo, Cvent, and other platforms for enterprise clients running international summits and multi-day conferences. Structured training sessions, not just documentation — which matters when your team includes people who aren’t event tech specialists. Enterprise teams have completed Bizzabo-to-InEvent migrations in as little as two weeks for straightforward setups. More complex programs with deep CRM integrations, custom workflows, and multi-event portfolios typically take four to six weeks. Ready to see how migration works for your specific setup? Book a walkthrough with InEvent’s onboarding team to map your Bizzabo configuration to InEvent’s platform. Which Bizzabo Competitor Should You Choose? A Quick Decision Guide You’ve read the reviews. You’ve seen the table. Now let’s make it simple. Here’s how to match your specific situation to the right platform. Choose InEvent if you need enterprise-grade hybrid and in-person events with offline check-in and local server sync, a full AI suite with 10+ tools including facial recognition check-in and platform-wide ChatGPT integration, native Microsoft ecosystem integration through Teams, Outlook, and Dynamics 365, the broadest security compliance stack on this list (SOC 2 Type II + GDPR + ISO 27001 + HIPAA + PCI DSS), and a dedicated project manager who knows your event before your attendees arrive. Choose Cvent if venue sourcing is a primary workflow for your team, you have a large procurement operation that needs access to the industry’s biggest supplier network, and you’re comfortable with enterprise-level pricing and a longer implementation timeline to unlock the full platform. Choose Swoogo if you want full control over registration design without needing engineers, transparent per-user pricing with unlimited events, and a lighter-weight platform that doesn’t require months of onboarding. Choose RainFocus if you’re running mega-conferences with 5,000 to 50,000+ attendees, you need deep behavioral analytics and Adobe or Salesforce marketing automation integrations, and your team has the technical resources to manage a complex implementation. Choose SpotMe if you’re in pharma or a regulated industry where native Veeva CRM integration, HCP compliance tracking, and multi-language support are non-negotiable requirements that generalist platforms can’t satisfy. Choose Webex Events if your organization already runs on Cisco infrastructure — Webex Meetings, Meraki networking, Duo security — and adding an event platform inside that existing governance framework matters more than best-in-class event features. Choose Whova if attendee networking and community engagement are your top KPIs, you’re running mid-market association or academic conferences with 500 to 3,000 attendees, and you value a polished attendee app over deep enterprise customization. Choose vFairs if your events are virtual-only — career fairs, expos, trade shows — and you want 3D environments with exhibitor booths. If any of your events have an in-person component, look elsewhere. Choose Swapcard if AI-powered B2B networking and lead scoring are the primary differentiators you sell to sponsors and exhibitors, and your events are conference or trade show formats where qualified meetings drive ROI. Choose EventsAir if you’re an association or government organization with public procurement requirements that values 35+ years of proven technology and strong onsite registration tools over cutting-edge AI or modern UI design. Not sure which fits? Bring your toughest use case to an InEvent demo . No sales pitch — just a live walkthrough mapped to your actual event requirements, timeline, and tech stack. Frequently Asked Questions About Bizzabo Competitors 1. What is the best Bizzabo competitor for enterprise events? InEvent is the strongest Bizzabo competitor for enterprise events in 2026. It’s the only platform on this list that combines offline check-in with local server sync, Microsoft Azure infrastructure, a 10+ tool AI suite including facial recognition check-in and platform-wide ChatGPT integration, and SOC 2 Type II + GDPR + ISO 27001 + HIPAA + PCI DSS compliance. Every enterprise client also gets a dedicated project manager and account manager — not a shared support queue. For teams running large-scale hybrid and in-person events where connectivity, security, and onsite operations complexity matter, InEvent fills the exact gaps where Bizzabo reaches its limits. 2. How much does Bizzabo cost compared to alternatives? Bizzabo doesn’t publish its pricing, but publicly available data puts the starting point at approximately $17,999 per year based on GetApp listings. InEvent starts at approximately $9,990 per year ( GetApp ), with custom enterprise plans and separate hardware rental pricing. Swoogo uses per-user pricing with unlimited events, making it one of the more budget-friendly options for teams running high volumes of smaller events. Cvent and RainFocus both use custom enterprise pricing that typically exceeds $20,000 per year depending on modules and event volume. The biggest pricing difference isn’t the starting number — it’s how predictable the total cost is after add-ons, overages, and hardware. 3. Which Bizzabo competitors support offline check-in? InEvent is the only major Bizzabo competitor that offers full offline check-in with local device sync, cached badge printing, and automatic data re-sync when connectivity is restored. Cvent’s OnArrival app has limited offline caching capabilities, and EventsAir offers partial offline registration based on its long history with in-person events. Every other platform on this list — Swoogo, RainFocus, SpotMe, Webex Events, Whova, vFairs, and Swapcard — requires persistent internet for check-in operations. If your events happen in venues with unreliable WiFi, this is the most important column in your evaluation. 4. Can I migrate my data from Bizzabo to another platform? Yes. Most modern event platforms accept CSV imports for attendee databases, and CRM integrations can be reconfigured during migration. InEvent’s onboarding team has helped enterprise clients migrate from Bizzabo in as little as two weeks for straightforward setups, including reconfiguring Salesforce and HubSpot integrations, rebuilding email automation workflows, and training teams on the new platform. More complex programs typically take four to six weeks. We covered the full migration process in the step-by-step migration guide above. 5. Which Bizzabo competitor has the best CRM integrations? InEvent offers native connectors for Salesforce, HubSpot, Dynamics 365, Marketo, and Veeva — without relying on Zapier or middleware. It also integrates with Amadeus and Sabre for travel data, which matters for international summit management . Cvent has strong native integrations with Salesforce, Marketo, and Eloqua. RainFocus stands out for its deep Adobe and Salesforce automation integrations. SpotMe’s native Veeva integration is the best in the category for life science teams. The right answer depends on your CRM — but if you’re evaluating on breadth of native connectors without middleware, InEvent and Cvent lead. 6. Is Bizzabo still a good platform in 2026? Yes. Let’s be clear about that. Bizzabo is a Gartner Magic Quadrant Leader and a Forrester Wave Leader. Their Klik SmartBadge technology is excellent for networking data and sponsor ROI measurement. Their CRM integrations with Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, and Eloqua are solid. Their branded event page builder is polished. For B2B marketing conferences in well-connected venues with strong WiFi, Bizzabo remains a very capable platform. The teams exploring alternatives aren’t leaving because Bizzabo is bad. They’re leaving because their needs have grown beyond what Bizzabo’s architecture currently supports — offline check-in for venues with unreliable connectivity, deeper AI tools for registration and onsite operations, private cloud hosting for regulated industries, and more transparent pricing at scale. 7. Which Bizzabo competitors support encrypted data storage and private cloud hosting? InEvent runs entirely on Microsoft Azure with SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and PCI DSS certification. Enterprise clients can deploy within Azure’s governance structures, and the platform supports dedicated hosting for organizations that can’t put attendee data on shared infrastructure. For a deeper look at how this works, read InEvent’s guides on encrypted data storage for events and private cloud hosting . Final Verdict: The Best Bizzabo Competitor Depends on Your Enterprise Needs Bizzabo is a strong platform. We said that at the top of this article and we’ll say it again here. It’s a Gartner Leader. It’s a Forrester Leader. Klik SmartBadges are clever technology. The CRM integrations are solid. If your events are well-connected B2B marketing conferences and Bizzabo’s pricing works for your budget, there’s no urgent reason to leave. But the enterprise event landscape in 2026 demands more than what Bizzabo currently delivers. Offline reliability when venue WiFi fails. AI-native tools that go beyond content generation into registration, check-in, matchmaking, and lead capture. Transparent pricing that doesn’t surprise you at renewal. Security compliance deep enough to satisfy government, healthcare, and financial services procurement teams. InEvent fills the exact gaps enterprise teams hit when Bizzabo reaches its limits. The AI suite is a generation ahead — 10+ tools versus a handful. The onsite stack includes hardware, software, and human support, not just software. The Microsoft Azure infrastructure means deployment inside enterprise governance structures. And the offline check-in with local server sync is the feature that matters most when everything else stops working. That last point is worth sitting with. Offline check-in is not a nice-to-have. It’s the difference between a smooth 8:00 AM registration and a 45-minute line that damages your brand before the keynote starts. It’s the difference between your registration team scanning badges confidently and your registration team writing names on blank lanyards by hand. Every platform on this list does most things well. Only one keeps working when the WiFi doesn’t. If your events happen in government and military facilities , municipal venues with public sector requirements , pharmaceutical campuses, convention centers at peak load, or international venues with unpredictable infrastructure — the choice becomes clear. title: Immatics Announces First Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Business Update
summary: SUPRAME Phase 3 interim and final analysis for PRAME cell therapy, anzu-cel, expected to be triggered in 2026, advancing toward the Company’s first commercial launch planned in 2027 Multiple key clinical data sets expected in 2026 across the portfolio, including four clinical-stage cell therapy and
body_text: Supporting Materials: PDF Version SUPRAME Phase 3 interim and final analysis for PRAME cell therapy, anzu-cel, expected to be triggered in 2026, advancing toward the Company’s first commercial launch planned in 2027 Multiple key clinical data sets expected in 2026 across the portfolio, including four clinical-stage cell therapy and bispecific candidates targeting cutaneous and uveal melanoma, gynecologic cancers (ovarian and uterine), head and neck cancer, and other solid tumor indications Phase 1 data readout with second-generation PRAME cell therapy, IMA203CD8, to be presented at the 2026 ASCO meeting, focusing on anti-tumor activity in gynecologic cancers Phase 1b clinical data from PRAME bispecific, IMA402, as monotherapy and initial data in combination with an immune checkpoint inhibitor at RP2D range expected in 2H 2026 First Phase 1 trial evaluating the combination of Immatics’ TCR bispecifics, IMA402 targeting PRAME and IMA401 targeting MAGEA4/8 in sqNSCLC, expected to begin in mid-2026 Cash and cash equivalents as well as other financial assets of $521.5 million1 (€453.6 million) as of March 31, 2026; cash reach projected into 2028 Houston, Texas and Tuebingen, Germany, May 12, 2026 – Immatics N.V. (NASDAQ: IMTX, “Immatics” or the “Company”), the global leader in precision targeting of PRAME with multiple clinical-stage programs spanning cell therapies and bispecifics, today provided a business update and reported financial results for the quarter ended March 31, 2026. “Immatics is entering a pivotal period as we continue to progress toward the pre-specified interim and final analyses from the Phase 3 SUPRAME trial of anzu-cel and actively prepare for commercialization in 2027,” said Harpreet Singh, Ph.D., Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Immatics. “At the same time, we expect multiple meaningful clinical readouts across our PRAME franchise in 2026 that continue to validate PRAME as an important target across multiple solid cancers, extending well beyond melanoma, and across two different therapeutic modalities. Immatics today is a company defined not only by compelling science, but by a diversified late- and mid-stage clinical portfolio, growing commercial readiness, and a clear strategy to translate innovation into meaningful patient impact.” First Quarter 2026 and Subsequent Company Progress PRAME Franchise – Cell Therapy Anzu-cel (IMA203) PRAME Cell Therapy – First Market Entry in Advanced Melanoma Anzu-cel (anzutresgene autoleucel), previously called IMA203, is Immatics’ lead PRAME cell therapy and is expected to be the Company’s first PRAME therapy to enter the market in advanced melanoma. The current addressable patient population for anzu-cel’s first target indications, second-line or later (2L) advanced cutaneous melanoma, as well as metastatic uveal melanoma includes ~9,000 patients 2 . Anzu-cel received Orphan Drug Designation and RMAT designation 3 from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of both cutaneous and uveal melanoma. Secondary analyses of Phase 1b clinical data on anzu-cel in advanced cutaneous and uveal melanoma will be presented during the Oral Abstract Session - Melanoma/Skin Cancers at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, with a focus on characterizing response dynamics. Phase 3 trial, SUPRAME, for anzu-cel (IMA203) in previously treated, advanced cutaneous melanoma Immatics’ global, randomized, controlled, multi-center Phase 3 clinical trial, SUPRAME, is currently ongoing to evaluate the efficacy, safety and tolerability of anzu-cel PRAME cell therapy as monotherapy vs. investigator's choice in patients with unresectable or metastatic cutaneous melanoma who have received prior treatment with a PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor. SUPRAME is designed to be an adequate and well-controlled clinical trial intended to generate data to support regulatory approval of anzu-cel. Primary endpoint for seeking full approval is blinded independent central review (“BICR”)-assessed (RECIST v1.1) progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints include overall survival (OS), objective response rate (ORR), safety and patient-reported outcomes measuring quality of life. Pre-specified interim and final data analyses are expected to be triggered in 2026 upon the occurrence of a defined number of events for PFS (progressive disease or death). The Company continues to expect BLA submission in the first half of 2027 and commercial launch of anzu-cel in the second half of 2027. Patient recruitment is currently ongoing in North America and Europe. Phase 2 cohort for anzu-cel (IMA203) PRAME cell therapy in patients with metastatic uveal melanoma A Phase 2 cohort to treat approximately 30 additional metastatic uveal melanoma patients is ongoing and being conducted at select centers in the U.S. and Germany with expertise in uveal melanoma. Data from the ongoing single-arm Phase 1b trial as well as the Phase 2 cohort in metastatic uveal melanoma are intended to support a potential label expansion for anzu-cel following expected initial approval in cutaneous melanoma. IMA203CD8 PRAME Cell Therapy (GEN2) – Expansion to all Advanced PRAME Cancers IMA203CD8 is the Company’s second-generation PRAME cell therapy product candidate being developed with the goal of expanding into all advanced PRAME cancers. Given its enhanced pharmacology profile, once the target dose is reached, the Company intends to pursue the clinical development of this product candidate with a tumor-agnostic approach, starting with gynecologic cancers (ovarian and uterine). Updated Phase 1a dose-escalation and Phase 1b dose-expansion data in gynecologic cancers at clinically relevant dose levels will be presented during the Rapid Oral Abstract Session – Gynecological Cancer at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting. The Company is on track to complete Phase 1a dose escalation and determine the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) in 2026. Further Updates on PRAME Cell Therapies PRAME cell therapy beyond melanoma and gynecologic cancers: updated Phase 1 data on PRAME cell therapies (anzu-cel or IMA203CD8 GEN2) in synovial sarcoma, further demonstrating the potential to address diverse tumor types beyond melanoma and gynecologic cancers, will be presented during the Rapid Oral Abstract Session - Sarcoma at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting. PRAME cell therapy using Immatics’ TCR in a pediatric patient with cancer: a late-breaking poster on a PRAME-directed TCR T-cell therapy using Immatics’ PRAME TCR administered under named-patient use in a heavily pretreated pediatric patient with extensive, multifocal nephroblastoma was presented at AACR Annual Meeting 2026. PRAME is expressed across multiple pediatric cancers, and these findings highlight the therapeutic potential of PRAME cell therapy in pediatric patients with solid tumors. PRAME Franchise - Bispecifics IMA402 PRAME Bispecific – Expansion to Earlier-Line PRAME Cancers To expand our PRAME opportunity to earlier-line PRAME cancers, the Company is developing its off-the-shelf, next-generation, half-life extended TCR bispecific, IMA402, as a monotherapy or in combination with standard of care, with a focus on melanoma and gynecologic cancers. In addition, Immatics is exploring the potential combination of IMA402 PRAME bispecific with IMA401 MAGEA4/8 bispecific in squamous non-small cell lung cancer (sqNSCLC) and potentially other solid tumor indications. IMA402 PRAME bispecific showed clinical proof-of-concept during the Phase 1a dose escalation trial in heavily pre-treated patients with solid tumors, including melanoma and ovarian cancer. Immatics expects to determine the final RP2D and present a clinical data update from a larger patient population, with an initial focus on melanoma and gynecologic cancers treated with IMA402 monotherapy or combination with an immune checkpoint inhibitor, in the second half of 2026. As part of its strategy to maximize the IMA402 opportunity, the Company is in the process of opening additional Phase 1b cohorts in mid-2026 across both earlier and later treatment lines. Based on the initial promising activity of IMA401 in head and neck cancer and sqNSCLC, Immatics believes it is uniquely positioned to assess the synergistic potential of combining two different bispecifics, IMA402 targeting PRAME and IMA401 targeting MAGEA4/8, with and without a checkpoint inhibitor. The Phase 1 trial evaluating the combination of IMA401/IMA402 in sqNSCLC is expected to commence mid-2026. IMA401 MAGEA4/8 Bispecific – Maximizing the Potential of Bispecifics Combinations Updated results for IMA401 targeting MAGEA4/8 across multiple cancers will be presented during the Developmental Therapeutics – Immunotherapy Oral Abstract Session at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting. IMA401 clinical development will focus on a combination approach with the Company’s PRAME bispecific, IMA402, to exploit synergistic potential and expanded patient reach. The Phase 1 trial evaluating the combination of IMA401/IMA402 is expected to commence with sqNSCLC in mid-2026. Corporate Development: In collaboration, Moderna and Immatics developed a cancer antigen therapeutic candidate under the Database Program, incorporating targets identified using Immatics’ XPRESIDENT® target discovery and validation platform and its bioinformatics and AI platform XCUBE®. The shared antigen therapeutic candidate owned by Moderna was submitted for IND, marking a key regulatory milestone under the Collaboration Agreement and triggering a milestone payment to Immatics. First Quarter 2026 Financial Results Cash Position: Cash and cash equivalents, as well as other financial assets, total $521.5 million1 (€453.6 million) as of March 31, 2026, compared to $539.6 million1 (€469.3 million) as of December 31, 2025. The decrease is the result of ongoing research and development activities, partially offset by the net proceeds of an at-the-market offering of $24.4 million1 net (€21.2 million) as well as changes in net working capital and foreign exchange rate differences. Revenue: Total revenue, consisting of revenue from collaboration agreements, was $8.7 million1 (€7.6 million) for the three months ended March 31, 2026, compared to $21.4 million1 (€18.6 million) for the three months ended March 31, 2025. The decrease is mainly due to a lower proportion of costs incurred relative to the overall project progress within the quarter. Research and Development Expenses: R&D expenses were $68.1 million1 (€59.2 million) for the three months ended March 31, 2026, compared to $48.2 million1 (€41.9 million) for the three months ended March 31, 2025. The increase mainly resulted from costs associated with the advancement of the product candidates in clinical trials, particularly the SUPRAME clinical trial. General and Administrative Expenses: G&A expenses were $16.7 million1 (€14.5 million) for the three months ended March 31, 2026, compared to $13.9 million1 (€12.1 million) for the three months ended March 31, 2025. The increase is driven by costs associated with early commercial activities supporting the planned market launch of anzu-cel (IMA203). title: How to Build a Property Management App (No Code)
summary: Build a property management app — tenant tracking, maintenance requests, rent collection, and lease management. Buildium costs $55-460/mo. Build your own for free.
body_text: The Tenant Lifecycle Every feature in the app maps to a stage in the tenant journey: Application → Screening: Collect applications, run background checks (integrates with Checkr or TransUnion), approve or decline. Move-in: Generate lease, collect security deposit, log unit condition with photos. Monthly operations: Rent collection, maintenance requests, communication. Lease renewal: 60-day notice, new terms negotiation, updated lease document. Move-out: Final walkthrough, deposit reconciliation, unit turnover checklist. Build the full lifecycle and you've replaced the spreadsheet, the email chain, and the paper folder in a single app. Step-by-Step Build with Blink 1 Set up properties and units Start with: "Build a property management app. Create a properties table with address, number of units, and property type. Create a units table linked to properties with unit number, square footage, rent amount, and current status (vacant, occupied, maintenance)." Blink provisions the database and builds the admin interface. Auth is built in — no Clerk or Firebase Auth setup. You're the owner; tenants can get their own login later. 2 Add tenant management Tell Blink: "Add a tenants table with first name, last name, email, phone, emergency contact, move-in date, and a foreign key to their unit. Show an active tenants list on the dashboard with their unit and payment status." Link tenants to units and you have the core data model. The admin panel guide covers dashboard layout patterns for multi-record management. 3 Add lease tracking Tell Blink: "Add a leases table with tenant ID, unit ID, lease start date, lease end date, monthly rent amount, security deposit amount, and a document upload field for the signed lease PDF. Show a renewal alert for leases expiring within 60 days." The 60-day alert alone saves the most common landlord mistake: missing a renewal window and losing a tenant to a month-to-month default. 4 Set up rent collection via Stripe Tell Blink: "Add Stripe ACH payments for monthly rent. Each tenant should be able to enter their bank account and set up automatic monthly payments. Log each payment in a rent_payments table with tenant ID, amount, payment date, and status. Send a payment confirmation email when a payment clears." Stripe ACH charges $0.80 per transaction. Buildium's ACH fee is $1.50 per transaction — nearly double. On 20 units with monthly payments, that's an extra $14/month in per-transaction fees alone. For more on Stripe subscription patterns, see the Stripe subscription guide . 5 Build the maintenance request system Tell Blink: "Add a maintenance_requests table with tenant ID, unit ID, description, priority (low/medium/urgent), status (submitted/in progress/resolved), assigned contractor, and resolution notes. Tenants should be able to submit requests from their portal. I should get an email notification for every new urgent request." Maintenance tracking is the highest-ROI feature for landlords. A logged, timestamped ticket trail protects you in disputes and keeps contractors accountable. 6 Build the owner dashboard Tell Blink: "Create a dashboard overview showing: total units, occupancy rate, rent collected this month vs expected, open maintenance requests by priority, and leases expiring in the next 90 days. Add a quick-search to find any tenant or unit by name or address." This is the control center. Blink handles the hosting — no Vercel config, no deployment pipeline. The app goes live on a custom domain immediately. A property management dashboard — occupancy status, rent collection, and maintenance tickets in a single view Blink Rent Collection via Stripe ACH Stripe ACH (Automated Clearing House) is the right payment method for recurring rent. Credit cards charge 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction — on a $2,000 rent payment, that's $58.30/month in processing fees. ACH caps at $0.80. Set up automatic monthly payments so tenants authorize once and pay every month without action. The system handles reminders, retries on failed payments, and late fee calculation. For late fees: build a scheduled job that checks rent_payments on the 5th of each month. If a tenant hasn't paid, add a late fee row and send a notification. Blink builds the logic — describe the late fee policy and it handles the implementation. Maintenance Request Workflow The maintenance flow has four stages, and tracking each one protects you: Submitted — Tenant fills out the web form (or SMS prompt if you build that). They describe the issue, attach a photo, and mark priority. In Progress — You assign the request to a contractor. The ticket logs the assignment with a timestamp. Awaiting Approval — Contractor completes the work. They log the cost and attach an invoice. You review before marking resolved. Resolved — Ticket closes with resolution notes, total cost, and resolution date logged. The timestamp trail is important: it documents how quickly you responded to each issue. That record matters if a tenant later claims a habitability issue went unaddressed. The Per-Unit Pricing Problem Here's why building your own makes financial sense at every portfolio size: Units Buildium AppFolio Blink-built app 5 units $55/mo (minimum) $280/mo (minimum) $0–$20/mo 25 units $55/mo $280/mo $0–$20/mo 100 units $460/mo $150/mo $20/mo Buildium's pricing starts at $55/month for up to 150 units on the Essential plan. AppFolio's pricing charges $1.50/unit/month with a $280 minimum — meaning you pay the same whether you have 1 property or 186 properties. A Blink-built app costs whatever Blink's plan costs. No per-unit pricing. No feature gating by tier. 43% of US rental housing is managed by landlords with fewer than 10 units — the per-unit model was never designed for this market segment. Per-unit pricing punishes growth — a flat monthly cost for a custom-built app is cheaper at every portfolio size from 5 to 100 units Blink What You Give Up Be honest about the tradeoffs. Commercial property management software gives you: Tenant screening integrations (TransUnion, Equifax) — you'd need to connect these yourself Pre-built legal forms for your state — you'd need to source and upload your own lease templates Mobile apps for tenants — Blink builds responsive web apps; a native iOS/Android app requires additional work Compliance with local landlord-tenant law updates — you're responsible for keeping your own forms current For an independent landlord managing 2–20 properties, the tradeoffs are worth it. For a property manager handling 500+ units with compliance staff, commercial software may still make sense. Frequently Asked Questions Yes. Blink builds responsive web apps that work on any device — phone, tablet, or desktop. No native app download required. Tenants access their portal at a URL you give them and submit requests from the browser on their phone. Add a security_deposits table with tenant ID, amount collected, collection date, and held balance. When a tenant moves out, the move-out workflow calculates deductions and generates a deposit reconciliation statement. Some states require deposits to be held in a separate escrow account — your accounting setup handles that outside the app. Yes. Add a property_owners table and link properties to owners. Each owner gets a login that shows only their properties. The role system controls what each user can see and edit. Blink's built-in auth handles multi-user access — no Firebase Auth configuration required. Yes, with additional fields. Commercial leases have different terms — triple net (NNN) calculations, CAM charges, percentage rent clauses. You'd add those fields to the leases table. The core architecture is the same; the data model is more complex. Describe your commercial lease structure to Blink and it builds the schema. Build a scheduled alert that fires 60 days before each lease end date and emails you with a renewal prompt. From there, you generate a new lease document, negotiate updated rent, and either renew or begin move-out process. Blink builds the alert logic — describe the trigger condition and timeline. Blink connects to external APIs. Checkr and TransUnion SmartMove both offer API-based background check integrations. Tell Blink to add a "Request Background Check" button to the tenant application flow and it builds the integration. You'll need an account with the screening service — the background check itself is not a Blink product.
